title: KVStore prefetch heuristics & eviction pattern triage - Nimbus Robotics
topics: quantization impact on memory and performance
summary: Deep technical session focused on a recurring production issue at Nimbus where their long-context chat workloads were triggering excessive KV store evictions and paging. Redwood SE walked through the runtime's eviction heuristics, prefetch options, telemetry needed to diagnose prefix hotspots, and tradeoffs between caching aggressiveness vs latency. Action items agreed: run a targeted benchmark with provided trace set, enable per-prefix eviction telemetry and short-term prefetch rules, and evaluate Dedicated deployment with VPC peering for lower cross-host egress variance.
next_steps: Redwood to share KV debug checklist and a trimmed trace set for reproducible benchmark - Morgan - by 2025-11-24
Nimbus to enable experimental prefetch flag in staging and report hit/miss metrics - Aisha - by 2025-11-28
Schedule 1-hour follow-up to review benchmark results and eviction heatmaps - Morgan/Priya + Nimbus - 2025-12-01

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-21 14:30 PST / Duration ~62m / Recording enabled. Attendees listed in metadata.

00:00 Morgan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, i think we have about an hour — quick intros?
00:08 Carlos (Nimbus): carlos here — we've been seeing this recurring issue where our chat assistant with long context (up to 60k tokens) causes weird latency spikes and then a wave of evictions, esp during bursts.
00:18 Priya (Redwood SE): ok, thanks carlos. can you sketch the infra very quickly — are you on hosted, dedicated, or a hybrid?
00:25 Carlos: currently hybrid. we started on the hosted api for prototyping, but for prod we've got a dedicated pool in our cloud account. traffic comes from a few regionally located robots and a central ingestion cluster.
00:36 Aisha (Nimbus): most inference is pinned to a 16k/32k context model quantized to int8 but we do occasionally route to a 64k variant for big sessions.
00:46 Morgan: got it. the symptom is eviction waves + paging to disk, which then causes higher latency for following requests?
00:51 Carlos: yes exactly — you'll see a normal latency tail then it rockets up to multiple seconds and some requests get retried. our ops chart shows KV cache hit ratio dropping during those windows.
01:02 Priya: ok, i'm gonna walk through the runtime behavior quickly. Our KV store uses an adaptive TTL + size-aware eviction. defaults bias toward recency (LRU-ish) but we also do prefix-aware eviction to avoid evicting frequently accessed prefixes. when you have a lot of unique prefixes or a burst with long unique session prefixes, that can thrash the cache.
01:24 Dmitri: when you say prefix, do you mean chat session id prefix or actual prompt prefix tokens?
01:30 Priya: session-level prefix — we key KV entries per session and per token block. so if you have many unique session ids, you get many cold prefixes. if those sessions interleave, you don't get good reuse.
01:40 Aisha: that's probably our case. robots open lots of ephemeral sessions for each interaction and many are one-off.
01:46 Priya: right. the runtime also has a paging mechanism — KV entries can spill to local SSD or a network storage depending on deployment. The spill threshold is tuned conservatively to avoid disk thrashing, but under sustained memory pressure we do page which creates the latency cliffs you described.
02:02 Morgan: two levers: reduce faux-unique prefixes (session reuse), or increase cache pressure tolerance (bigger pool or different eviction policy). also prefetch can help if you can predict next-prefix access.
02:12 Aisha: we tried increasing pool size but that was expensive and still saw issues during bursts. we do want to avoid paying up-front for huge headroom.
02:21 Priya: understood — so let's discuss heuristics. first, prefix coalescing: if you can map ephemeral sessions into a stable user/device id or bucket sessions by device, you get much better reuse. second, prefetch rules: if session pattern indicates sequential chunk accesses, enable a small lookahead prefetch for next token blocks. this trades a small extra memory for fewer page-ins.
02:44 Carlos: the tricky part is that sometimes robots stream multiple concurrent conversations. coalescing isn't always possible because two distinct conversations happened around the same time but share a device.
02:53 Priya: in that case a hybrid approach helps: keep session granularity but add an access-frequency filter so the prefetch triggers only if prefix has > N hits in last M seconds. it avoids polluting cache with one-off prefixes.
03:06 Morgan: can you quantify N and M? what did you test in other customers?
03:12 Priya: typical safe defaults we suggest: N=3 hits in 30s, prefetch one subsequent block, prefetch depth=1, prefetch disabled for prefixes with lifetime < 10s. but those numbers are workload-dependent.
03:26 Dmitri: ok — about eviction policy. is it plain LRU? we see a hot prefix getting evicted while low-value prefixes stay.
03:33 Priya: it's weighted LRU with a frequency boost for prefixes with consistent reuse. but signatures can get noisy — if your telemetry doesn't surface per-prefix hit rates, the adaptive weight can be misled. we've seen degenerative cases where many near-simultaneous new prefixes bump out the boost windows causing hot prefix eviction.
03:53 Aisha: what telemetry should we turn on to capture that?
03:56 Priya: enable per-prefix counters (hits, misses), eviction reason tags (age / size / low frequency), spill events with latency histograms, and the active set size over time. We'll provide the exact metrics names in the playbook.
04:10 Morgan: also add the KV cache TTL distribution and the sequence length distribution. that helps correlate long-context sessions to eviction events.
04:18 Carlos: one of our ops graphs shows TTLs being honored but still evicting early — could that be an artifact of wrong size accounting?
04:25 Priya: possible. size accounting can be off if quantization changes footprint post-warmup or if objects aren't coalesced. quantized weights mean KV block sizes vary and the runtime relies on approximations unless you enable precise accounting. precise accounting adds a small CPU overhead but helps with eviction correctness.
04:42 Aisha: what about paging — you mentioned disk spill. is that to local ephemeral SSD or NFS? ours is currently to network attached storage behind VPC.
04:51 Priya: network spill adds variability. disk spill to local NVMe is >100x faster than network spill; network spill latency depends on cross-host throughput and encryption overhead. For on-prem/VPC customers we recommend local SSD spillback or Dedicated nodes with co-located storage.
05:08 Dmitri: is that something Redwood Dedicated offers?
05:11 Morgan: yes, Dedicated lets you choose co-located NVMe backing and we can deploy in your VPC with peered networking to reduce egress variance. that's a larger commitment but often reduces tail latency by removing network spill.
05:24 Leah (Security): for VPC peering we need to understand encryption, KMS access, and also audit trails — any implications to how KV telemetry is transported?
05:33 Priya: we stream compact metrics to the control plane; for Private/VPC deployments we can use customer-managed endpoints and TLS with mutual auth, plus optional KMS-wrapped sink. Audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. We'll share the security doc.
05:47 Morgan: let's talk about long-context specifics: you said sessions up to 60k tokens, but model variants up to 64k — that means KV footprint per session is large. If you have many concurrent 60k sessions, memory multiplies quickly.
06:01 Carlos: we typically have a distribution: 70% short sessions, 25% mid (8-20k), 5% long (40-60k) but those long ones are heavy hitters when they overlap with bursts.
06:12 Priya: for that distribution we recommend a mixed strategy: preserve hot prefixes for long sessions by pinning their KV entries for a short grace period once they pass a token threshold, plus aggressive eviction of prefixes that remain single-hit. Pinning avoids losing the KV that long runs rely on.
06:27 Aisha: would pinning blow memory? how do you unpin?
06:31 Priya: pinning is time-limited (e.g., 5-10 minutes) and gated by a scoring function. it only applies when session length > X tokens and hit rate > Y. again, we'll give a sample scoring formula.
06:44 Morgan: can we discuss prefix reuse hotspots? your logs show some prefixes accessed extremely frequently while others never. That could suggest our adaptive weight isn't catching the pattern quickly enough.
06:56 Priya: yes. hotspot detection can be improved with a two-tier cache: a small lightning cache for ultra-hot prefixes (very low-latency lookup) and a larger backing cache. That reduces eviction pressure but adds complexity and marginal memory overhead.
07:14 Carlos: what about prefetch misprediction? if we prefetch aggressively and predictions are wrong, that can cause pollution and worsen evictions.
07:23 Priya: hence the frequency threshold. Also, prefer depth=1 prefetch with early abort if no subsequent access within a few hundred ms. For async prefetch, we also have circuit breakers to stop prefetching under sustained low hit ratio.
07:38 Dmitri: curious about monitoring: do you provide tracing hooks for prefix-level traces?
07:42 Priya: yes, we have a tracing hook that emits a compact prefix timeline for sampled requests with KV lookups, hits, misses, and eviction events. Sample rates default low for perf reasons but can be increased for debug sessions.
07:56 Aisha: ok that will help. we'll bump sampling in staging for a day to capture an incident.
08:02 Morgan: on quantization: int4 reduces model weight memory, but KV block sizes are influenced by activations and cache serialization format. When you quantize aggressively, you change the footprint unpredictably which can confuse size heuristics. Our runtime supports quantization-aware accounting if you set the flag.
08:21 Carlos: what about the CPU overhead of precise accounting you mentioned?
08:24 Priya: rough ballpark: 2-5% CPU increase on the host for precise accounting, but that eliminates a lot of eviction-induced rework. Worth it for production where evictions cost many seconds of latency.
08:37 Morgan: batching — small note: if you increase batch size aggressively to amortize GPU cost, you might lengthen the time a prefix stays in active memory before it's eligible for eviction, which can be beneficial, but it increases per-request queuing latency. So it's a balance.
08:54 Carlos: our SLA is 300ms p95, but we accept up to 800ms occasionally. during these paging events we hit multiple seconds.
09:03 Priya: so aim for conservative batching and stronger prefix retention rather than huge batch sizes. Also set a fallback model (smaller context) for requests that would otherwise trigger a page-in — degrade gracefully.
09:16 Aisha: interesting — fallback model rules might be the fastest operational fix. but we need to ensure quality fallback is acceptable.
09:23 Morgan: we can help with an A/B test that routes traffic to fallback when predicted page-in cost > threshold. We'll provide the routing rule template.
09:33 Dmitri: network-wise, are there recommendations for VPC egress sizing to avoid variable spill latency?
09:37 Priya: yes: provision dedicated egress bandwidth for your inference pool, use peered subnets in same AZ when possible, and prefer local NVMe for spillback. If you must use network storage, ensure bandwidth >= 5x the expected burst throughput to avoid queueing. We'll attach recommended numbers.
09:55 Carlos: security question: do eviction traces ever contain PII? our prompts sometimes have user data.
10:01 Leah: yes we need strong controls.
10:04 Priya: we never emit full prompt contents in telemetry by default, only hashed prefix identifiers and sizes. For audits, you can enable masked samples under customer-managed encryption and consent. We'll include options in the security doc.
10:18 Morgan: quick recap: enable per-prefix telemetry, test prefetch flags with N=3/30s default, try pinning for long sessions, run benchmark traces in staging, consider Dedicated with local NVMe for spillback if network spill is root cause.
10:33 Carlos: sounds good. we'll prioritize telemetry and a short staging run.
10:38 Aisha: one practical question — do you have a small script or tool to generate the eviction heatmap we can run?
10:44 Priya: yes — we'll drop a python notebook and a flamegraph script into the shared folder. it will take sampled traces and output an eviction timeline and per-prefix heatmap.
10:54 Morgan: perfect. i'll share the links after call — the playbook includes exact metric names and a sample config for prefetch and pinning.
10:59 Andy (PM): timeline wise, if we get the staging run by next week can we expect guidance on config changes for prod by 12/8?
11:07 Morgan: yes that's attainable. we'll do an initial analysis by 12/1 and provide recommended knobs by 12/8.
11:15 Carlos: ok thanks everyone. that was helpful. any last questions?
11:19 Aisha: none. thanks.
11:21 Morgan: thanks all, i'll send notes + artifacts. goodbye.

Post-call notes: references shared during the call: "KV debug playbook" (link uploaded to shared folder), "prefetch notebook" (link), sample traces file: nimbus-traces-2025-11-18.tar.gz, security doc: redwood-private-vpc-security.pdf.

End of transcript.
